name: Politics as fundamentally a question of power, not of abstract right
plain_explanation: Slogans like 'right will prevail' obscure the fact that whichever side wins does so because it commands superior power; though appearing virtuous can itself be a source of power (since it wins public support), this is a contingent, propagandistic advantage rather than proof that virtue always triumphs.
precise_definition: Russell's synthesis of Machiavelli's implicit view: 'The question is ultimately one of power. To achieve a political end, power, of one kind or another, is necessary... it is an advantage in propaganda to seem more virtuous than your adversary, and that one way of seeming virtuous is to be virtuous,' but this is qualified by the observation that those already in power can control propaganda to appear virtuous regardless of their actual conduct.
why_it_mattered: Provides Russell's bridge between the 'immoral' and 'moral' halves of Machiavelli's doctrine, and generalizes it into a broader claim about the historical role of virtue as a (contingent) instrument of political success.
historical_origin: Illustrated by the growing power of the Church in the eleventh-thirteenth centuries and the success of the Reformation in the sixteenth, both attributed partly to a public perception of comparative virtue.
examples: No one could mention Alexander VI's sins in a New York or Boston public school, illustrating how those in power control propaganda about their own virtue
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly political: connects the appearance of virtue to religious and political legitimacy.
